title: My Koinly or CoinTracking report doesn’t add up
excerpt: Why a software-generated report shows gains you don’t recognise, which reconciliation errors are common and how they’re corrected before you file with the Spanish Tax Agency (AEAT).

hero.h1: Your report shows a gain that doesn’t add up
hero.subheading: You’ve run your data through Koinly, CoinTracking or similar, and the result looks nothing like what you think you made. Before assuming the mistake is yours, it’s worth checking how the software has handled four or five specific situations.

cita.texto: An automated report is a starting point, never the deliverable.
cita.pie: Software reads a lot of files quickly. What it doesn’t do is make decisions. And in a real portfolio, most of the work is decisions.

sections.body:
The software hasn’t got it wrong in the sense of malfunctioning: it has done exactly what it knows how to do. Faced with a situation it can’t resolve with certainty, it applies a default value. And that default is usually the most conservative option for the software, which is rarely the most accurate one for you.

The usual result is an inflated gain. Not because you made more, but because the report counts as sales things that aren’t sales, and values at zero things that cost you money.

This can be fixed as long as the report hasn’t been filed. Once it reaches the AEAT it becomes your return, and correcting it is a different job — longer and more expensive. That’s why this page exists: for the moment before.

sections.entrada: A portfolio with transfers between your own wallets and tokens received from staking. This is how an automated report reads it, and this is how it looks after reconciliation.

filas.concepto: Gain according to the automated report
Less: internal transfers counted as sales
Less: recovered acquisition cost of staking tokens

bullets: Internal transfers treated as disposals: you send funds from your exchange to your cold wallet and the report records it as a sale. It’s by far the biggest source of phantom gains.
Zero acquisition cost: tokens received from staking, airdrops, forks or liquidity rewards that the software values at zero, so that when you sell them the entire proceeds count as gain.
Token spam processed as income: on chains such as Solana or BSC there can be thousands of junk records cluttering the entire portfolio.
Mis-valued swaps: swapping one token for another is taxable as an exchange of assets, but the value assigned to it depends on the reference price, and not all price oracles agree.
Duplicates across sources: the same transaction read from the exchange CSV and from the on-chain wallet, counted twice.
Time zones: timestamps in different time zones that change the order of transactions and, with it, the result of the FIFO calculation.
Gaps treated as if nothing happened: the period covering a closed exchange simply doesn’t appear, and with it goes the acquisition cost of whatever you bought there.

steps.title: We start from your report, not from scratch
steps.body: It saves us the data-ingestion stage and makes the work cheaper. What we do is audit the reconciliation, not redo what’s already right.

steps.title: We isolate transfers between your own accounts
steps.body: We identify who owns each destination address and mark those transfers as internal. This is where most of the difference shows up.

steps.title: We recover the missing acquisition cost
steps.body: For each token received without a purchase, we determine its value on the date it was received and document the price source.

steps.title: We filter spam with judgement
steps.body: Not with an automatic list: we check which entries are third-party noise and which are real transactions that look like noise.

steps.title: We deliver the difference, explained
steps.body: What changes compared with your report, why, and with what documentary support. So you can defend every line.

items.q: So are Koinly and CoinTracking wrong?
items.a: No. They’re good tools doing what they do: processing volume. The problem isn’t the tool, it’s treating its output as the final result instead of as the starting point. We use similar tools ourselves; the difference lies in what is done afterwards.

items.q: How much does a review cost compared with starting from scratch?
items.a: A review is usually considerably cheaper, because the data ingestion has already been done. The cost depends on how many transactions need reclassifying, and that becomes clear after a first pass. We give you a price before we start.

items.q: I’ve already filed the report with the tax authorities
items.a: Then it’s a different job and is best approached from the litigation side: correcting something already submitted requires a documented explanation of the discrepancy with what you filed. It can be done, but it’s more delicate.

items.q: Do you need access to my accounts?
items.a: No. We work with the export of your report, your CSV files, read-only API keys and public wallet addresses. Never private keys.

items.q: And if the review shows the report was right?
items.a: We’ll tell you, and you’ll have the peace of mind of having checked, plus the criteria memo that supports each decision. There isn’t always an error, but knowing there isn’t one is worth something too.

cierre.h2: Before you file it, have someone look at it
cierre.body: Tell us which tool you used to generate it, how many transactions it contains and which platforms and chains you use. After a first pass we’ll know whether there is a difference and how big it is.
